sections.h2: Where to file a Clark County deed
sections.html:
The Clark County recorder is located in the A.B. Graham Building at 31 North Limestone Street in Springfield, OH 45502. Phone 937-521-1705 to reach the office, or send a fax to 937-328-4620. Bring the deed, the parcel numbers and a way to pay for the fees listed below.

Because the auditor and treasurer share the building, a single visit can cover the value statement, any tax payoff and the recording. Owners in New Carlisle, the villages and the townships use the same counter. The county's public records page links to a Recorder's Office Title Search and a Land Records and Property Alerts page, which lets you review any recorded deed or lien before listing or signing.

Ohio fixes recording costs in section 317.32. Every charge has two equal halves, a base fee kept by the recorder and a housing trust fund fee. A county is also allowed a preservation surcharge, up to $5 on each instrument. The statute says "up to," so find out the exact local amount and ask for the current sheet.

Clark County recording charges set by state statute
Recorder serviceBase portionTrust fund portion
Recording and indexing, pages one and two$17$17
Every added page or fraction of a page$4$4
Certified copy per page$1$1
Seal on a certification50 cents50 cents
Marginal reference (separate instrument)$2$2
Photocopy at the counter, per page$1$1

Pages are sized 8.5 by 14 inches, with the caption page counted, so a third page raises the bill.

sections.h2: What the auditor does before recording
sections.html:
Before recording, the deed goes to the auditor (section 319.202). The buyer or the buyer's agent files a value statement, either electronically or as three paper copies, and the auditor stamps the fee onto the deed. The auditor is at 31 N. Limestone Street, phone 937-521-1860. Charges that may apply:

  • The statement fee, from section 319.54(G)(3): $1, or ten cents per $100 of value (counting any part of $100), whichever is higher.
  • An optional transfer tax under section 322.02. It tops out at thirty cents per $100 and requires two public hearings before a county adopts it. The auditor can say whether Clark County has done so.
  • The recorder's own fees, shown in the table, which you pay separately at that counter.

Sellers cover the auditor's fee and any transfer tax, so look for both on your closing statement. When the property is a residential rental, the endorsement adds a reminder that the buyer owes the auditor landlord information under section 5323.02. If you are a landlord selling, tell the buyer about this early, since it becomes the new owner's task during closing.

sections.h2: Tax questions on the value statement
sections.html:
The value statement also works as a tax checkpoint. The buyer records the seller's answer under section 323.152: either no reduction applies to this year's or last year's taxes, or a sworn estimate of the reduction. Homestead and owner-occupancy credits are typical.

A second question covers land valued for farm use. If the parcel was enrolled, the buyer must acknowledge a possible recoupment charge once it stops qualifying. Roughly a quarter of residents live in rural areas. If you own acreage, ask the auditor about enrollment ahead of signing.

sections.h2: Deeds exempt from the auditor's fee
sections.html:
Certain transfers owe no fee under section 319.54(G)(3). The filer writes the reason on the filing. A Clark County owner might meet one of these:

  • Government deals: any deed going to or coming from a federal, state or local body.
  • Tax or assessment sales for delinquency.
  • Deeds written only to secure a debt or to release one.
  • Property worth $100 or less.
  • A handover where no money or other tangible value changes hands and it is not a gift.
  • Leases, except one renewable forever.

More cases exist beyond these. For an exempt deed, the auditor supplies the exemption form that replaces the value statement.

The public records page leads to a recorder title search and to a land records site with property alerts. Sign an alert up for a name or parcel and you get a notice when a paper is filed against it. This helps most with rentals, estate houses and vacant houses, where no one may be around to see a suspicious filing.

Title companies run that same search ahead of closing. When an old mortgage was paid but the lender never recorded a release, the release must be filed first and costs its own recording fee.

sections.h2: Recording a sale step by step
sections.html: Someone, usually the title agent or an attorney, drafts the deed with the legal description and each parcel number. You sign in front of a notary. Then the buyer's side finishes the value statement and takes it, with the deed, to the auditor. The auditor endorses the deed, and the grantor pays the fee and any transfer tax. After that the deed goes to the recorder, who counts the pages, collects the base and trust fund fees and any surcharge, and records it. Hold on to a copy of the recorded deed and the receipt, since the title company may ask for either later, and check that the recording date matches your closing date. If a lender is paid off in the same closing, confirm that its release is recorded too.

Clark County covers 403 square miles of west central Ohio. It has two cities, Springfield and New Carlisle, and Springfield sits roughly 45 miles west of Columbus and 25 miles northeast of Dayton. Population was 135,340 in July 2025, down 0.5 percent from April 2020. There are 61,550 housing units, and owners occupy 69.4 percent of homes. The median owner-occupied value is $169,900 and median monthly rent is $872. Most city residents attend Springfield City Schools, though parts of the north go to Northeastern Local or Northwestern Local and parts of the west and south to Clark-Shawnee Local.

sections.h2: Getting ready for a quick sale
sections.html:
A cash closing still goes through the auditor, then the recorder. The title agent normally carries the papers, but you can walk them over yourself. For a house that came through an estate, confirm that the person signing has authority from the probate court. Clear liens and back taxes before closing so the recording goes smoothly.

Three questions are worth settling before the signing date. Is there a county transfer tax? What will the recorder charge for the page count of your deed? Does any old mortgage still lack a recorded release? A cash sale skips lender underwriting, so these county steps are usually the only ones that set the timeline.

faqs.q: Which building houses the Clark County recorder?
faqs.a: The A.B. Graham Building, 31 North Limestone Street, Springfield, OH 45502. The office phone is 937-521-1705.

faqs.q: What does Ohio charge to record the first two pages of a Clark County deed?
faqs.a: The state charges $17 as a base fee and another $17 for the housing trust fund. On top of that a county may add as much as $5, so ask the Clark County recorder what applies.

faqs.q: Does Clark County levy a real property transfer tax?
faqs.a: A county may adopt one, up to thirty cents per $100 of value. Whether Clark County has is a question for the auditor. The seller pays it with the auditor's fee.

faqs.q: Are Clark County deeds searchable online?
faqs.a: Yes. Use the Recorder's Office Title Search or the Land Records and Property Alerts page, both linked from the county's public records page. Alerts tell you when something is filed under your name or parcel.

faqs.q: Do I go to the auditor or the recorder first with a deed?
faqs.a: Start at the auditor. That is where the buyer's value statement is filed, and the auditor endorses the deed before the recorder sees it.
